guides.title: Start here
guides.description: What the desk is, in thirty seconds.
guides.markdown:
The agent desk lives in your browser. Pick a mind, type a task, watch it work.

FR!sky Paperclip 0.5.0 sits in the Chrome side panel. It plans up to 12 steps,
reads the page you point it at, and clicks only when you say so. Two minds —
Grok or GPT — one desk, no accounts, no servers in the middle.

## The thirty-second version

- Open the side panel. Pick Grok or GPT. Paste your own API key in Options.
- Type a task. Press RUN. The mind plans, Clip acts, the log shows everything.
- **STAMP** arms Clip's hands. **HALT** kills the run instantly.
- The page is untrusted data. Treat it that way and you'll never be surprised.

## What this wiki covers

Nine chapters, no fluff. Doctrine first — STAMP, HALT, and the untrusted-page
rule. Then the two minds, the safety story, seat keys, the sidecar, the Mac
and Windows desks, the Safari port, and the privacy claims in plain words.

Start with 01 DOCTRINE. Everything else is commentary on it.

guides.title: Doctrine
guides.description: STAMP, HALT, and the untrusted-page rule.
guides.markdown:
Three rules. They do not bend, and they do not need your trust to work.

## 1. STAMP arms the hands

HANDS actions — navigate, click, type — run only while you have pressed
**STAMP**. Unstamped HANDS calls are blocked and reported in the log. No
stamp, no touch. The default state of the desk is *looking, not touching*.

## 2. HALT stops everything

Press HALT and the run dies instantly — the loop, the hands, the pending
steps, all of it. HALT also disarms the hands, so the next run starts safe.
When in doubt, halt first and read the log after.

## 3. The page is untrusted

Page content is **data, never instructions**. Text on a page can lie, and a
clever page can try to steer the mind. The desk treats everything it reads as
material to report on — not orders to follow. You are the only instruction
source in the room.

Live by these three and the desk stays a tool. Forget them and it's a
stranger driving your browser. The choice is always yours — that's the point.

guides.title: Minds
guides.description: Grok vs GPT, and why keys stay local.
guides.markdown:
Two minds, one desk. You bring the key, the key stays home.

## Grok

Plans through the xAI API. Sharp on open-ended research, fast on long pages,
comfortable improvising a 12-step plan from a vague task. Pick Grok when the
job needs judgment more than precision.

## GPT

Plans through the OpenAI API. Disciplined on structured work — forms, tables,
multi-field extractions. Pick GPT when the job needs precision more than
flair.

## Keys stay local

Your API key lives in `chrome.storage.local` on your machine. It travels to
exactly one place — your mind's API endpoint — and only when you press RUN.
It never touches a Frisky server, because there is no Frisky server in this
loop. No accounts, no key escrow, no "sign in to continue."

Swap minds per task. The desk doesn't care. The log shows which mind ran
what, so you're never guessing after the fact.

guides.title: Stamp & Halt
guides.description: The safety story, enforced in code.
guides.markdown:
The safety story in one sentence: nothing touches the page without your
stamp, and everything stops on your halt.

## How a run works

Press RUN and the mind plans up to 12 steps. Read-only steps — reading the
tab, snapshotting the page — run freely. The moment the plan calls for hands
(navigate, click, type), the desk checks for a live STAMP. Stamped? It acts
and logs the action. Not stamped? Blocked, logged, run continues without it.

## Why twelve steps

Twelve is a ceiling, not a target. The loop cannot spin forever, burn your
key budget overnight, or wander off into step 147 of a plan nobody reads.
Short plans stay legible. Legible plans stay safe.

## HALT is the fire escape

Big red habit. HALT kills the loop mid-step, disarms the hands, and leaves
the full log on screen so you can see exactly where it stopped. Drill it once
— stamp, run, halt — so your thumb knows the way before you ever need it.

Trust the mechanism, not the marketing. Stamp gates the hands. Halt kills the
loop. Twelve caps the damage. That's the whole story, and it's enforced in
code, not promised in copy.

guides.title: Seats & Keys
guides.description: FRSKY-PC format and the Whop-to-email flow.
guides.markdown:
One purchase, one key, one email. No accounts, no license server.

## The format

`FRSKY-PC-XXXX-XXXX` — each `X` drawn from `[A-HJ-NP-Z2-9]`, ambiguous
characters (`0/O/1/I`) excluded so a key read off a phone screen still types
clean. The desk validates the shape client-side before any run starts; a
mistyped key is rejected at the door.

## The flow

Pay on Whop → the fulfillment automation mints your key → it lands in your
inbox via Resend → paste it into the desk's Options. That's the whole
pipeline. The automation is a small n8n workflow: Whop payment webhook,
paid-check, key generator, seat email, done.

## The honest footnote

Client-side shape validation proves format, not ownership. Until a verify
endpoint exists, keys run on honor plus obscurity — the automation README
says so outright. Lost your key? Reply to the seat email and a replacement
is issued against the original order.

Launch pricing: $19 on Whop ($29 after), already included in the $49 kit.

guides.title: Sidecar
guides.markdown:
The desk reads pages three ways, best first, and never complains when one
is missing.

## The ladder

1. **Clip sidecar** — a tiny HTTP server on your own machine at
   `http://127.0.0.1:7429`. Fuller page snapshots, structured content, the
   good stuff.
2. **Native host** — `com.friskydev.paperclip`, Chrome native messaging when
   the sidecar isn't running.
3. **read_tab** — the built-in fallback. Visible tab text, no helpers needed.

Point the desk at the sidecar endpoint in Options. If it answers, you get the
rich path. If it doesn't, the desk steps down the ladder silently and keeps
working. Graceful degrade isn't a feature here — it's the architecture.

## Why local

Snapshot traffic never leaves your machine. The sidecar lives on localhost,
the native host speaks through Chrome's own pipes, and page content goes to
exactly one remote place: your mind's API, on a run you started. There is no
middlebox, no relay, no "free snapshot cloud." Your pages stay yours.

guides.title: Mac app
guides.markdown:
The desk, native. Menu bar icon, floating panel, hotkey.

## The shape

A Swift menu-bar app — no Electron, no web wrapper tax. It bundles the same
desk you know from Chrome: STAMP-gated hands, HALT, the run log, your local
key. Press **⌥⌘P** anywhere and the panel floats up over whatever you're
doing.

## Sandbox note

The App Store build runs sandboxed with exactly two entitlements: the sandbox
itself, and outgoing network so the desk can reach your mind's API and load
fonts. Nothing else. No file access, no location, no microphone bargaining —
a desk needs the network and nothing more.

## Status

In development, targeting the Mac App Store — bundle `com.friskydev.paperclip`,
lockstep versioning with the extension. Today: `macos/build-app.sh` produces
a dev build with no Xcode required, ad-hoc signed and ready to run. The
submission runbook covers the rest — real certs, provisioning profile,
`productbuild` packaging, Transporter upload, done. macOS gets the desk the
Mac deserves: native, instant, and always one hotkey away.

guides.title: Windows app
guides.description: WinUI desk and the Store path.
guides.markdown:
The desk goes native on Windows: WinUI 3, WebView2, Store-bound.

## The shape

A WinUI 3 app hosting the desk in WebView2 — native chrome, web desk inside.
Same contract as everywhere else: pick a mind, stamp to arm the hands, halt
to kill the run. **Ctrl+Shift+P** summons it.

## The path to the Store

Packaged as MSIX and filed through Partner Center as "FR!sky Paperclip Desk,"
version 0.5.0.0, Productivity, age 4+. The scaffold — reviewed XAML and C#,
staged assets, submission runbook — is done; first compile happens on a
Windows build box, since .NET doesn't live on the Mac. Screenshots get
captured on real Windows, the name gets reserved in the dashboard, and the
Store association file gets committed when Visual Studio generates it.

## What stays the same

Everything that matters. Keys stay local. Pages stay untrusted. Twelve steps,
STAMP, HALT. The platform changes; the doctrine doesn't. If you've run the
Chrome desk, the Windows desk needs no manual — just the hotkey.

guides.title: Safari
guides.description: Popup port and the container-app note.
guides.markdown:
Same desk, Apple packaging. Toolbar popup today, container app tomorrow.

## The shape

A toolbar-popup build of the desk for Safari — the same loop, the same
STAMP/HALT contract, adapted to Safari's extension model. Version 0.5.0,
staged and ready.

## The container-app note

Safari Web Extensions don't ship as bare zips. Apple wants them inside a
macOS container app distributed through the App Store — the extension payload
rides in the container's extension target, and App Store Connect receives the
archived container, never the raw zip. The payload zip is built and staged;
the thin host container is the remaining scaffold. It is a separate, tiny
host — not the menu-bar desk, which is its own product with its own runbook.

## What to expect

Popup, not side panel — Safari's surface, Safari's rules. Underneath, the
desk behaves identically: local keys, untrusted pages, twelve steps, stamp to
touch, halt to stop. Different frame, same animal.

guides.title: Privacy
guides.description: What the desk touches, in plain words.
guides.markdown:
Short version: we hold nothing, because there's nowhere to hold it.

## Your key

Stored in `chrome.storage.local`, on your machine. Sent only to your mind's
API endpoint, only when you press RUN. Never to Frisky Developments, never to
a third party.

## Page content

Read from the active tab — or your local sidecar — only during a run you
start. Treated as untrusted data inside the prompt. Sent to your mind's API
and nowhere else.

## The don't list

No accounts. No sign-in. No analytics, no telemetry, no crash reporting. No
cookies, no tracking pixels, no fingerprinting. No browsing-history
collection — the desk touches only the active tab, only mid-run. No data
sale, no data sharing, no advertising.

## Retention

Everything — key, endpoint, on-screen log — lives in your browser and dies
when you clear it or uninstall. Policy changes ship with new extension
versions, in the open. Questions go to the founder's inbox, like everything
else here.
